newsitem.title: UK: Corporate branding a risk, but so are old brands.
newsitem.headline: Corporate branding a risk, but so are old brands.

text.p: Companies that spend millions on new corporate images are taking a risk, but it's often a bigger risk to do nothing, corporate identity specialists said on Wednesday.

"It is hugely expensive to launch a new identity but sometimes companies have no choice if they want to be perceived as modern forward thinking organisations," Richard Watson, a consultant to the design industry, told Reuters.

British Airways Plc, which has launched a 60 million ($100 million) facelift that replaces its traditional British flag motif on its planes with ethnic art, is the latest in a long line of companies which have introduced new identities.

"I think it's a sound strategy. It signals that BA wants to be a global airline. I think in ten years' time they will drop the word British from their name and become something like Global Airways," said Adrian Day, managing director of Landor, an international design firm.
A new corporate identity such as BA's is expensive because the new look has to be applied to everything from its planes to stationery.

Watson said he expected BA to get the kind of criticism from consumers and the media that other big companies like British Telecommunications Plc and the British Broadcasting Corporation got when they launched major rebranding exercises.

"I'm sure people will criticise BA just as they criticised British Telecommunications when it introduced its new look and when the BBC straightened the letters in its name. People will say, 'How can sticking a few pictures on planes cost 60 million pounds?'" said Watson.
"What they don't understand is that a company like BA would have to spend that sort of money painting its planes anyway and that it will be phased in over a number of years," said Watson.
High costs are just one aspect of launching a new identity. Companies must also ensure that they meet consumer expectations and can deliver all that they promise.

"The most risky thing about a major identity project is if the company itself doesn't have a clear picture of where it is going or what if it wants to achieve," Kate Manasian, a director of Wolff Olins, a design company, told Reuters.
"If a new identity signals that the company is great, but its levels of service don't live up to it, then it will have no credibility with consumers," she said.
Most industry experts said they could think of few instances in which big companies have launched a new image -- and things had gone disastrously wrong.
"It's not as risky as you might imagine because these things are researched to death," said Andy Milligan from Interbrand, a brand consultancy company.
Experts say one company which launched a new brand, got it wrong and subsequently had to ditch the project was telecommunications company Hutchinson Whampoa.

"It launched a mobile phone company called Rabbit. The branding wasn't wrong but the product and the timing was wrong and it didn't live up to expectations. When they got it right, they launched the Orange phone company, which is very successful," said Manasian.

Milligan said, "Some people may think that Pepsi's decision to change its identity from red to blue last year was a failure because they have suffered a sales dip. But it's not about immediate sales. It's about implementing a long term strategy."
